statement: The system shall provide residents with a reliable way to monitor their home environment from one place.
The system shall help residents feel safer.
The system shall enable residents to respond quickly when something changes.
Security shall be the top user goal.
Stable control of temperature and humidity shall be the second user goal.
Convenient control of lighting and small appliances shall be the third user goal.
The system shall support regular residents or general users.
General users shall be able to view status and control everyday devices in their own home, including lights, climate, and appliances.
General users shall not be able to change system-wide settings or device configuration.
Technicians shall be able to access configuration and maintenance functions.
Technicians' permissions shall be limited to technical setup and diagnostics unless the resident specifically allows full daily use control.
Broader access must be explicitly approved by the resident or a master user.
Broader access should be temporary by default.
Broader access should be tied to a specific purpose such as installation or troubleshooting.
Broader access should expire automatically after a set time or when the task is completed.
The system should log what the technician accessed or changed during the period of broader access.
The system shall store the home profile for homes.
The system shall store user identity.
The system shall store user contact details for notifications.
The system shall track the device type for devices and sensors.
The system shall record who triggered a control action for devices and sensors and when the action was triggered.
The system shall generate alerts for intrusion or security faults.
The system shall generate alerts when temperature moves outside set ranges.
The system shall generate alerts when lights are left on unexpectedly.
The system shall generate alerts for device failures.
The system shall send the most urgent alerts immediately to the resident.
The web interface shall work on current major browsers.
The system shall remain usable even if the home network is slow.
The system shall deliver critical alerts quickly.
Sensors and controllers shall be assumed to depend on local power and connectivity.
The system shall provide recovery behavior after outages.
The system shall maintain backups of configuration and logs.
Retention and notification handling shall comply with local privacy rules.
The system shall support residents, master users, and technicians in performing needed actions with home devices.
The web side of the system shall work with sensors and controllers.
The system shall support security needs.
The system shall support comfort needs.
The system shall support device control needs.
The current home control setup is fragmented.
People use separate thermostats to control temperature.
People use separate light switches to control lighting.
People use appliance timers to control small appliances.
Some people use a basic alarm app for home security.
There is no single place to see all home control information or control it together.
DigitalHome should bring home security, temperature, humidity, lighting, and small appliance functions into one web interface with the sensors and controllers tied in.
The system shall replace separate apps and manual checks for security and climate control.
The system shall provide clearer access for master users and technicians when configuration or troubleshooting is needed.
The system shall provide basic alerts.
The system shall provide history so users can see when something changed or when a device went out of range.
The system shall provide role-based access control.
DigitalHome shall provide the main functions needed from the home user side.
The first release shall include a single web interface.
The system shall allow residents to open one place and quickly see the current state of the home.
The interface should feel simple and immediate.
The system shall not require residents to jump between different device-specific tools.

The web interface shall allow the resident to drill into each area after viewing the summary screen.
The resident shall be able to drill into the security area.
The resident shall be able to drill into the climate area.
The resident shall be able to drill into the lighting area.
The resident shall be able to drill into the appliances area.
The resident shall be able to make changes from each drilled-in area.
The web interface shall show the result of a change right away so the resident knows the system responded.
The system shall help residents monitor the home and control the main factors that affect comfort and safety.
The system shall support monitoring and control of security.
The system shall support monitoring and control of temperature.
The system shall support monitoring and control of humidity.
The system shall support monitoring and control of lighting.
The system shall support monitoring and control of small appliances.
The system shall allow people to react to alerts.
The system shall allow people to make changes remotely through a web interface.
The system shall cover normal day-to-day home management.
The system shall cover unusual situations where a door or window is opened.
The system shall cover unusual situations where a room gets too hot or humid.
The system shall cover unusual situations where lights are left on.
The system shall cover unusual situations where a device needs to be switched off.
The system shall coordinate between the web system and the devices installed in the home.
The system shall not add additional home environment domains unless there is a clear need identified during design or by users.
The system shall allow additional domains to be considered as extensions later if something else comes up.
The system shall support typical private residences, including apartments and single-family homes.

The system shall not target commercial buildings or anything outside normal residential use.

Dorms are out of scope for now.
Similar nonstandard residential places are out of scope for now.

The system may allow friendly display names.

The system shall explain failures in plain language rather than only providing a code or technical message.

The message for residents shall stay simple.
Technicians shall be able to see more detail for troubleshooting.
When a command is accepted, the interface shall immediately show that it is in progress so the user knows the request went through.
The quick and unambiguous feedback requirement is especially important for security or temperature changes.
Manual commands should take priority over automated rules, especially when a resident or master user is acting intentionally.

Current device values should remain available as long as the device is active.
Sensor history should be retained long enough to support troubleshooting and trend analysis.
The archive or deletion policy must be verified with the business team.

Technicians shall be able to remove devices.
Technicians shall be able to calibrate sensors.
Technicians shall be able to verify controller operation.
Technicians shall be able to run diagnostics.
Technicians shall be able to run connectivity checks.

Technicians shall be able to view logs.
Technicians shall be able to view error details.
Technicians shall not be able to manage resident preferences.
Technicians shall not be able to manage daily automation choices.
Technicians shall not be able to manage personal schedules.
Technicians shall be able to maintain the system.
Technicians shall not be able to use the system like a resident.
Technicians shall not be able to change private household settings.
If the system is unsure during device pairing, it shall stop short of fully enrolling the device and ask the installer to manually confirm the device type, zone, or function.
If the system is unsure during device pairing, it shall leave the device in a pending setup state rather than guessing and placing it in the wrong room or control category.
For technicians, the system shall explain what was ambiguous so they can correct it quickly.
The system shall support exclusions and limits on monitoring and control scope.

Technicians should only be able to apply or lift exclusions temporarily while doing installation, maintenance, or troubleshooting.
If a technician bypasses an exclusion, the bypass should be time-limited.
If a technician bypasses an exclusion, the bypass should be clearly logged.
If a technician bypasses an exclusion, the bypass should be visible to the master user afterward.
A technician should not be able to make long-term changes to privacy or notification behavior alone.
The environment shall not have major interference or dead spots that would break sensor communication.
If the network is weak, the installer shall flag it before finishing setup so it does not become a support problem later.
At installation, the system shall verify that the hub can reach the internet and the required DigitalHome web services.
At installation, the system shall verify that inbound or outbound connections are not blocked by the home network.
At installation, the system shall verify that the hub can communicate with the in-home devices it is supposed to manage.
At installation, the system shall verify that the hub can communicate with the in-home devices it is supposed to manage either directly or through the local controllers.
If the installation-time checks fail, setup shall pause or remain in a limited mode until the installer fixes the network path.
The coordination context should serve residents first in practice.
The coordination context should support day-to-day home management through residents' personal interface.
Master users should have extra coordination and configuration rights for household-wide settings.
Technicians should use the coordination context only for setup and support.
Technicians should not use the coordination context to change resident routines.
Residents should control usage.
Master users should control broader policy.
Technicians should be limited to maintenance-related actions.
Technicians shall be allowed to fix connectivity or calibration issues.
Technicians shall be allowed to verify alert delivery.
Technicians shall be allowed to make temporary maintenance changes when needed.
Technicians shall not be able to create resident schedules unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.
Technicians shall not be able to alter resident schedules unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.
Technicians shall not be able to create scenes unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.
Technicians shall not be able to alter scenes unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.
Technicians shall not be able to create permissions unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.
Technicians shall not be able to alter permissions unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.
Technicians shall not be able to create long-term automation rules unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.
Technicians shall not be able to alter long-term automation rules unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.
The system shall treat master user permissions as higher priority than technician actions.
A master user shall be able to override a technician when there is a conflict.
If a resident is actively using a device, the technician’s maintenance action shall be blocked or deferred unless it is a safe diagnostic action that will not disrupt operation.
Any simultaneous change shall be resolved by locking the setting or prompting for approval.
The system shall not allow both simultaneous changes to go through.

If both the master user and the technician are touching the same setting, the system should default to giving the master user immediate control and should block the technician or ask the technician to wait.
If the technician already has an active maintenance session, the system should lock the setting for normal changes and require the master user to explicitly approve any override.
The system does not define any case in which the technician overrides the master user for this kind of change.
The system should allow residents to change the friendly name they see in the home app.
The system shall alert when temperature or humidity readings move outside preset safe ranges for a sustained period.
The system shall be able to trigger automatic control actions such as HVAC, humidifier, or dehumidifier adjustments before a comfort issue occurs.
The system shall react immediately to security events such as intrusion, forced entry, or tamper detection.
The system shall send security alerts right away and escalate to emergency response only for the most serious security cases.
The system shall allow a short delay or confirmation window for automatic actions only if doing so does not reduce safety.
Residents or master users shall be able to override comfort-related automatic actions.
Residents or master users shall not be able to override security emergency response after it has been triggered.
If a temperature or humidity condition clears and then comes back, the system shall retry the check.
For security events, the system shall have almost no waiting before responding.

The guided setup shall explain what each main area does in plain language.

The web interface shall allow the resident to skip the tour or onboarding tips once the resident is comfortable.
The web interface shall enable a new resident to understand the basics and start controlling the home without needing a manual.

Onboarding should be optional and should not gate access to basic use.

If a reading is stale, missing, or clearly out of range for the device, the dashboard shall flag it rather than present it as normal.
